meta.title: Transportation and infrastructure, 17 days of posts
meta.subject: transportation and infrastructure policy in Texas — TxDOT's Unified Transportation Program and funding, highway expansions like I-45 in Houston, transit including Houston METRO, toll roads, airports and ports, and the fights over what gets built
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 17, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas transportation and infrastructure, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Transit and rail deserve more
lanes.description: Texas pours money into roads while METRO buses, passenger rail and high-speed rail between the big cities are starved, which hurts people who can't or don't want to drive.

lanes.label: Highway expansion is progress
lanes.description: Widening, flyovers, elevated lanes and new connectors are the way to ease congestion and serve Texas's growth, and project milestones show the work is delivering.

lanes.label: TxDOT can't build or manage
lanes.description: TxDOT is slow, tone-deaf and stuck in a rut: it answers congestion by adding lanes, delays projects like US 380, and gets mocked even for its own messaging.

lanes.label: Megaprojects cost too much
lanes.description: The 10-year Unified Transportation Program puts huge sums into a few showpiece freeway projects such as burying I-345 in Dallas, so taxpayers should question the price tag and the priorities.

lanes.label: Texas tolls are a ripoff
lanes.description: Texas toll roads are expensive and often unavoidable, so drivers pay twice and Texas shouldn't be seen as the low-cost state.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Marc Gravely
posts.text:
Texas's new road plan lists $1.65 billion to bury 1.4 miles of freeway in Dallas.

That's more than $1 billion a mile.

The road is I-345, the elevated stretch between downtown and Deep Ellum, running from I-30 to Woodall Rodgers. It's the second-largest project in the 10-year plan, which carries about $95 billion in transportation investments across the state.

TxDOT's design rebuilds it below street level, in a trench with no frontage roads and new city streets crossing over the top. Dallas City Council backed that approach in May 2023.

There's no start date yet. TxDOT has previously estimated about five years of construction once the money is lined up.

But the reason this stretch matters starts long before the freeway:

In the 1870s, two railroads met just east of downtown Dallas, and Deep Ellum grew up around the junction.

It became a home of early blues. Blind Lemon Jefferson and Lead Belly played there. In 1937, Robert Johnson recorded in a makeshift studio in downtown Dallas.

Then the roads came. In 1969, an elevated stretch of Central Expressway wiped out the 2400 block of Elm Street, which many saw as the heart of the neighborhood.

The elevated freeway now called I-345 opened in 1973, standing between Deep Ellum and downtown.

In 1973, Texas lifted a freeway over Deep Ellum. Fifty-three years later, it plans to spend $1.65 billion putting it underground.

posts.name: 𝐃𝐚𝐫𝐤 𝐇𝐚𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐝
posts.text:
Who is responsible for California's failures?

Let's just say it straight because no one else will.

Decades of one-party Democratic rule in Sacramento.

Homelessness, unaffordable housing, stores locking up shampoo behind glass, people leaving the state in U-Hauls, needles on playgrounds  none of that happened overnight. It happened over 20+ years of total control.

California hasn't had a Republican governor since 2011. Democrats have a supermajority in both the Assembly and the Senate. They own every committee, every budget, every policy. You can't blame anyone else when you have had absolute power that long.

Look at the results:

Homelessness:
We spend $20+ BILLION on homelessness and the number keeps going UP. Over 180,000 homeless in California  that's 30% of the entire country's homeless population in one state. Sacramento keeps passing "Housing First" programs with no accountability, no drug treatment requirement, no mental health mandate. You get a tent and a check and they call it compassion. It's not compassion. It's abandonment.

Housing:
The most beautiful land in America and your 28-year-old can't afford a 1-bedroom. Why? Because Sacramento made it impossible to build. CEQA lawsuits, endless permits, environmental reviews that take 10 years, $100k in fees before you even break ground. They talk about "affordable housing" while killing every single affordable project with red tape. A state that can't build housing should not lecture anyone about anything.

Quality of Life:
 Energy bills double the national average. Gas $2 more than the rest of the country. The worst roads, rolling blackouts in the tech capital of the world, shoplifting decriminalized up to $950 so businesses just leave. Oakland, San Francisco, LA  places people used to dream about moving to are now places people are desperate to leave.

Democratic leadership traded common sense for ideology. They want to be the most progressive state in the country more than they want to be a functional state.

They chose open-air drug use over treatment.
They chose illegal encampments over safe neighborhoods.
They chose bureaucracy over building.
They chose high-speed rail to nowhere over fixing dams and roads.

You cannot run the 4th largest economy in the world on press releases and virtue signaling. You need results.

And after 15 years of Democrat trifecta control, the result is this: The highest cost of living, the highest poverty rate when you factor in cost of living, and 800,000+ people who left in the last 3 years alone.

California isn't failing because of climate change, or Republicans, or Trump, or Texas. California is failing because the people who have been in charge for decades made it fail.

Until Sacramento is willing to admit that, nothing will change. https://t.co/qBeTMUQqnb
